key: traffic constable at a Bengaluru signal
name: ch12_signal_excuse_fine
alt: A traffic constable at a red signal writes a fine while a scooter rider argues that the road was empty.
scene: A street-level view of a Bengaluru traffic junction at mid-morning. On the left a tall signal pole glows with a bright red light, and beyond it the cross road is completely empty, just a zebra crossing and a distant tree. In the centre a young man in his mid-20s, grey hoodie, open-face helmet pushed up, sits astride a teal scooter that has stopped just past the stop line. He leans forward with one palm spread out towards the empty road, mouth open in an eager excuse, while his speech bubble shows an empty road with a small arrow, his argument that nobody was coming. On the right stands a traffic constable in a khaki uniform with a white cap and a whistle on a cord, holding a challan pad and pen. His eyebrows are drawn together and his mouth is a hard flat line; he is already writing, and a red exclamation badge floats over his head to show that the excuse has turned a possible warning into a point of pride for him. A thin dashed arrow runs from the rider's bubble to the challan pad, showing that the argument itself caused the fine. Bright daylight, slightly tense mood. Labels: "EXCUSE" above the rider's speech bubble, "FINE" printed in large letters on the top sheet of the challan pad.

name: ch12_late_home_say_it_first
alt: A son arriving late at night admits his mistake first, and his mother at the door softens and offers him dinner.
scene: A warm night scene at the front door of a small Indian apartment. On the left wall beside the door hangs a round clock whose hands clearly point to ten o'clock, and a small inset card near it reads "8 PM" with a red cross through it, the time he had promised. In the open doorway stands a mother in her early 50s in a plum cotton saree, hair in a bun, one hand still on the door frame; her face is caught at the exact moment it changes from worry to relief, eyebrows softening. Facing her on the doormat is her son, about 22, in a mustard t-shirt with a backpack on one shoulder and his phone in his hand, head slightly bowed, one hand on his chest as he speaks first. His speech bubble shows the clock with an arrow from eight to ten and a phone with a small cross, meaning he admits everything before she can begin. Her answering bubble, on the right, shows only a steel thali with rice, dal and two rotis and a small question mark: have you eaten? Behind her the warm yellow light of the hall spills out, with a dining table and a covered dish visible inside. A soft orange glow and calm mood after the tension. Label: "SAY IT FIRST" across the top centre of the picture.

key: A tailor in Chandni Chowk delivers
name: ch12_tailor_short_sleeve
alt: A tailor holds up a wedding kurta and points out its short sleeve himself while the customer relaxes.
scene: Inside a narrow old Delhi tailoring shop with a wooden counter, a black sewing machine on the left, and shelves of folded cloth bolts in teal, amber and coral behind. Behind the counter stands the tailor, a man in his 50s with spectacles, a measuring tape draped round his neck and a white kurta, holding up a cream wedding kurta with gold embroidery at the collar by its shoulders. With one finger he points at the left sleeve, which ends visibly shorter than the right; a small inset with a ruler shows the gap and reads "1 cm". His expression is open and apologetic, eyebrows raised, a slight smile. On the right, across the counter, the customer, a young man in his late 20s in a blue shirt, had come in ready to argue: a faded red storm cloud above his head is dissolving, and his hand is raised in a relaxed wave, as if saying it is hardly visible. Between them on the counter lie a pincushion, chalk, a pair of large scissors and a paper receipt. A small green tick floats near the kurta to show the problem is being settled kindly. Warm afternoon light through the shop door. Label: "MY MISTAKE" above the tailor's head, near the top left.

key: electricity bill comes in at triple
name: ch12_bill_it_was_me
alt: In a joint family the grandfather waves a huge electricity bill and the eldest son raises his hand to say it was him.
scene: A joint-family living room in the evening with a sofa, a ceiling fan and a doorway on the right that opens into an empty guest room where a wall air conditioner is still running, with blue cold-air lines flowing out over an unused bed. In the centre sits the grandfather, in his 70s, white kurta and dhoti, spectacles, in a cane armchair, holding up a long electricity bill on which a big "x3" is printed in red. Thin dashed arrows from him point in turn at three suspects on the left, each with a small red cross: two children on the floor holding phones, a new geyser on the wall, and an electricity meter box by the door. Standing to the right of the grandfather, between him and the guest room, is the eldest son, about 40, in a teal shirt, with one hand raised and the other on his chest, face calm and honest. A dashed arrow runs from the running AC to the son, linking him to the real cause. The children look up relieved. The grandfather's expression is a tired sigh rather than anger, and a small inset shows a timer switch with a spanner, the job he is given. Soft tubelight glow. Label: "IT WAS ME" in a speech bubble above the son's raised hand.

key: World Cup semi-final after a top-order
name: ch12_captain_on_me
alt: A cricket captain at a press conference points to himself instead of blaming the pitch, the dew or the toss.
scene: A post-match press conference room after a lost semi-final. A long table covered in a dark teal cloth runs across the lower middle of the picture with two microphones and a water bottle on it. Behind the table sits the captain, a man in his early 30s in a blue team training jacket with no logos, short beard, serious and steady, one hand flat on his chest. Above and to the left of him float three faded, greyed-out thought icons with red crosses through them: a cracked pitch strip, water droplets for dew, and a tossed coin, the excuses he does not use. A bold teal arrow curves from those crossed icons back round to his own chest. In the foreground at the bottom left, two reporters seen from behind hold up a phone and a notebook, and a camera on a tripod stands on the right. Behind the captain, on a plain backdrop, a small faded scoreboard panel reads "LOST". On the far right, a small inset shows the dressing room: three teammates in the same jackets standing together with their arms round each other's shoulders, looking towards their captain. Bright, flat press-room lighting, sober but proud mood. Label: "ON ME" in large letters above the captain, centred near the top.

key: Two brothers in a Kerala family
name: ch12_brothers_onam_verandah
alt: An elder brother who travelled by bus sits on his younger brother's verandah and apologises while their children play cricket.
scene: A Kerala house in the late afternoon of the Onam festival: a sloping red-tiled roof, white walls, wooden pillars and a low verandah, with a coconut palm on the left and a round flower pookalam of orange, yellow and red petals on the ground in front of the steps. On the far left, at the edge of the road, a small bus is pulling away, with a dashed path running from it to the verandah, showing the elder brother came by himself. On the verandah sit the two brothers side by side. The elder, in his 50s with grey hair, wears a cream mundu and a plum shirt; he leans towards his brother with his palms open, head lowered, apologising. The younger, in his mid-40s, in a white mundu and teal shirt, has turned towards him, one hand starting to reach for his shoulder, his face softening. A small inset bubble above them shows a broken line between two little houses being joined back with a green tick. In the yard on the right, four children from both families, in bright clothes, play cricket with a bat, a ball and a small set of stumps made from sticks, one child mid-swing and another running. Golden light, festive and warm. Label: "I WAS WRONG" in the speech bubble above the elder brother.

name: ch12_society_chat_chai
alt: A secretary answers an angry chat message about parking by inviting the neighbour for Sunday chai, where they redraw the plan together.
scene: A split picture divided by a thin vertical line. LEFT half: a large smartphone fills most of the panel, showing a generic group chat with plain grey and white bubbles and no app logo. The top message, from a neighbour shown as a small round avatar with a frown, is outlined in coral with a red exclamation badge and contains a tiny parking diagram with an angry face. Below it, a longer reply from the secretary, avatar with spectacles, is outlined in teal and ends with a small chai cup icon and a calendar square reading "SUN". RIGHT half: the same two people on Sunday morning at a small round table on an apartment balcony with potted plants. The secretary, a man in his 60s in a cream kurta and spectacles, sits relaxed holding a glass of chai, nodding. The neighbour, a woman in her late 30s in a coral kurta, has arrived with a rolled sheet and is pointing at a new parking plan spread on the table, with neat rectangles for cars and a green tick. The old plan lies crumpled to one side. Two steaming chai glasses and a plate of biscuits sit between them. Soft morning light, calm and friendly. Labels: "ANGRY POST" at the top of the left half, "SUNDAY CHAI" at the top of the right half.

key: A chaiwala hands you a glass
name: ch12_two_chaiwalas
alt: Two chai stalls side by side: one chaiwala argues with a customer who leaves, the other admits the mistake and pours a fresh glass for a returning customer.
scene: A split street scene in the early morning, divided by a thin vertical line, two almost identical roadside chai stalls with a kettle on a small stove, a steel tray of small glasses and a jar of biscuits. LEFT half: the chaiwala, a man in his 40s in a grey vest with a towel on his shoulder, stands with his arms crossed and his chin up, frowning; his speech bubble shows a pointing finger and a red cross, meaning you never said it. The customer, a young office-goer in a blue shirt with a laptop bag, is turning away and walking off, leaving the full glass with a sugar-cube icon on the counter. RIGHT half: the second chaiwala, similar age, in a mustard vest, is laughing, tipping the wrong glass out into a bucket with one hand while the other pours a fresh stream of chai from the kettle into a new glass, and a small timer badge reads "30 s". The same customer stands at his counter smiling, and a small calendar strip under the stall shows the next few mornings with green ticks, showing he keeps coming back. Gentle golden steam rises from the kettle. Labels: "ARGUE" at the top of the left half, "ADMIT" at the top of the right half.
